Graphs, trending, and engagement with restraint

Screens 11–15 and 19–22. The workbook calls leaderboards "the most dangerous mechanic on this list — it directly rewards measurable output over correct output" and says streaks are "actively harmful" in research. Both are built here, off by default, scoped, and carrying the argument against themselves on the screen.

WHAT THIS IS FOR
Reviewer conflict-of-interest checking, mostly. The reviewer invitation screen queries this graph to exclude anyone you have co-authored with in five years — which is exactly the window most journals use.
WHAT IT IS NOT FOR
Not a centrality score, not an influence ranking, not a "your network is smaller than average" nudge. A co-authorship graph rendered as a status object is a straight line to the vanity metrics this platform refuses.

12 TRENDING IN YOUR FIELD (E12) 680 × 560 · trending by reuse, not by views
TRENDING · CELL BIOLOGY · 7 DAYS ranked by reuse and replication
WHAT "TRENDING" MEANS HERE
An item trends when it is forked, reused, replicated or cited — acts that cost the other person something. Views, clicks and shares are not counted at all, because they are free and therefore gameable.

No global trending. No cross-field "hot right now". Trending is scoped to a field you actually work in, because a platform-wide trending list is a popularity contest that quietly tells every small field it does not matter.

THE PRIVACY RULE BEHIND THIS
The workbook flags reader-level tracking as a privacy problem and prescribes institution-level aggregation. So:
The institution is named. The person never is.
Fewer than three downloads from one institution in a month reports as "a group in Switzerland".
Readers can browse without being counted, and are told so once.

13·19 THE TWO DANGEROUS MECHANICS — STREAKS (K01) AND LEADERBOARDS (K05) 1440 × 640 · both off by default, both arguing against themselves
SETTINGS · ENGAGEMENT MECHANICS two features the workbook names as harmful in a research context · both shipped off, with the reasoning shown
13CONTRIBUTION STREAK · K01OFF
Show me a contribution streak
A consecutive-day counter on your dashboard, visible only to you.
READ THIS BEFORE TURNING IT ON
Loss aversion makes streaks the strongest retention mechanic known. In research it is actively harmful: it rewards daily output, and good science is intermittent. A week of reading, a month of a failing experiment, and a fortnight of writing are all zero-activity periods that produce the best work.
IF YOU DO TURN IT ON
Private. It never appears on your public profile.
Never linked to publication output — no streak counts papers.
A broken streak is shown as a gap, not a failure. No "you lost your streak", no flame going out.
No streak leaderboards exist, at any scope.
Squares are weighted by contribution type, so a trivial edit does not look like a replication.
19LEADERBOARD · K05OFF · OPT-IN PER COMMUNITY
WHY THIS IS NOT GLOBAL AND NOT PUBLICATION-BASED
A global leaderboard ranked on output is the most dangerous mechanic available to a research platform: it rewards measurable output over correct output. The person who publishes six thin papers outranks the person who spent the year replicating someone else's result and finding it did not hold. So: opt-in only, scoped to a single community, and never based on publication counts.

People who have not opted in leave visible gaps in the ranking rather than being silently compressed out. A leaderboard that looks complete when it covers 1.4% of a community is a lie about the community.
Axes are all contribution-to-others. Answers accepted, replications run, reviews completed. There is no leaderboard on papers, citations, h-index, downloads or reputation total — and no way for a community organiser to create one.

QUIET HOURS · ON BY DEFAULT
08:00 – 19:00
Push is suppressed 19:00–08:00 local and all weekend, from the first day. You opt in to being reachable at night, not out of being disturbed.
No artificial urgency anywhere. No "3 people are waiting", no countdown timers, no red dots for things that are not addressed to you. If a notification would not matter tomorrow morning, it does not go out tonight.
